q: What effective (radial location, safety factor q, T_i) did Huang et al. actually use when they quote 'analytically determined the on-axis continuum frequency to be 90 kHz' — because a pure on-axis (q≈1) evaluation of the Turnbull/Gorelenkov BAE-gap formula gives ~236 kHz, and the paper's 90 kHz is only reproducible if q≈2.5 (i.e. the value is evaluated at the mode-peak radius, not at r=0)?
basis: Independent v3 reproduction: BAE-gap formula ω = c_s sqrt(7/4 + T_e/T_i)/(qR_0) at ST40 params gives 236 kHz at q=1 and 95 kHz at q=2.5. The paper's own ALCON continuum (Fig. 3 left) shows the BAAE gap at intermediate ψ, not at the magnetic axis, so the '90 kHz on-axis' phrasing is inconsistent with the mode's actual radial position.
next_steps: Ask the authors for the exact substitution used, or re-derive the near-axis continuum-equation solution of Gorelenkov 2007 for this equilibrium and check whether q appears explicitly. A short note clarifying the effective q would remove a 2.6× ambiguity in the analytic prediction.

q: Why do GTC-MHD (122 kHz) and NOVA (68.8 kHz) disagree by nearly a factor of 2 for the same ST40 equilibrium, when both codes are solving ideal-MHD Alfvén-wave equations? Is the discrepancy entirely due to the two different Grad–Shafranov solvers (XMAP vs. NOVA's q-solver), or is part of it numerical dispersion in the antenna-scan vs. eigenmode-code methods?
basis: Paper attributes the discrepancy to G-S solvers but its own §4 admits 'both equilibria remain self-consistent within their respective formulations' and the continuum shape difference is 'localised' to the core. Yet the frequency shift is nearly 2×, which is too large to be purely core equilibrium reconstruction sensitivity for a mode that lives at intermediate ψ.
next_steps: Run a third independent G-S solver (CHEASE or ESC) on the same TRANSP profiles and re-run both eigenmode codes on all three equilibria. If a large frequency shift remains for a fixed equilibrium, the numerical eigenmode method is the primary cause, not the equilibrium.

q: Does replacing the isotropic-Maxwellian EPs with an anisotropic slowing-down NBI distribution (with realistic pitch-angle scattering off the co-current 55 kV D beam) recover the experimentally observed persistence of the BAAE, or is a nonlinear treatment absolutely required?
basis: Paper §5 explicitly flags the isotropic-Maxwellian approximation as a candidate explanation for the qualitative failure to reproduce the mode with EPs. It also says extending to a slowing-down (still isotropic) distribution 'still fails' — but does NOT test an anisotropic slowing-down. This is the single missing test that would separate 'wrong EP distribution' from 'wrong physics (i.e. needs nonlinear)'.
next_steps: Repeat the GTC gyrokinetic run with a beam-projected slowing-down distribution ~ exp(-|v_perp/v_beam|^2/Δ^2) H(v0-|v|)/v^3, matching the ST40 55-kV geometry. GTC already supports anisotropic loads in principle.

q: How sensitive are the BAAE frequency, growth rate, and mode structure to a radially-varying Z_eff(r) instead of the spatially-uniform Z_i used in the paper (motivated by the C6+ impurity profile actually measured by charge exchange)?
basis: Paper §3 admits 'GTC employs a spatially uniform effective charge Z_i while the experimental impurity profile varies radially, this approximation leads to the slight deviation between the simulated and experimental ion density profiles'. Impurity dilution affects both n_i (hence v_A) and the effective plasma pressure, both of which enter the BAAE dispersion.
next_steps: Instrument GTC with a Z_eff(r) profile (or as a first check, perturb Z_i by ±10 % and re-run) and quantify the induced shift in BAAE f and γ. The paper's ~15 % NOVA↔GTC frequency spread could be partly explained by such a systematic.

q: What single quantitative diagnostic — E∥/E∥,es, δW radial distribution, δB∥/δB⊥, or continuum-crossing signature — most robustly distinguishes a BAAE (Huang et al. this paper on ST40) from an interchange-like LFM (Choi et al. 2021 on DIII-D) when both share thermal-ion drive and δB∥ ≈ 0.5·δB⊥? Without such a diagnostic the two identifications are not distinguishable from observation alone.
basis: Paper §5 explicitly notes the ST40 mode has 'properties and excitation mechanisms similar to the LFM in the DIII-D tokamak which is an interchange-like mode driven by the pressure gradient of thermal plasmas' — and yet the two are assigned different names (BAAE here, interchange there). This is a taxonomic issue for the whole field.
next_steps: Design a matrix of GTC runs varying pressure gradient, temperature gradient, δB∥ inclusion, and equilibrium shape, and identify which diagnostic changes discontinuously across the BAAE↔interchange boundary. Propose a community-standard mode-identification protocol.
